entries.12bb2b5a09a4f19e709bd95cac9b6e83c1b1c017: <div sID="gen8840" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="7" osisID="Neh.7" sID="Neh.7"/> <div eID="gen8840" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8841" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8842" type="x-p"/> The success of one good design for God and our generation should encourage us to proceed and form some other; Nehemiah did so, having fortified Jerusalem with gates and walls, his next care is, I. To see the city well kept, <reference osisRef="Neh.7.1-Neh.7.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. To see it well peopled, in order to which he here reviews and calls over the register of the children of the captivity, the families that returned at first, and records it, <reference osisRef="Neh.7.5-Neh.7.73">ver. 5-73</reference>. It is the same, in effect, with that which we had, <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.1-Ezra.2.62">Ezra ii.</reference> What use he made of it we shall find afterwards, when he brought one of ten to live in Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Neh.11.1">ch. xi. 1</reference>.
entries.2d5fe458577f8a62b9ce8d8273ac5ff72fad0d93: <div eID="gen8842" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8841" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Completion of the Wall. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 445.)</title> <div sID="gen8843" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now it came to pass, when the wall was built, and I had set up the doors, and the porters and the singers and the Levites were appointed, <hi type="super">2</hi> That I gave my brother Hanani, and Hananiah the ruler of the palace, charge over Jerusalem: for he <hi type="italic">was</hi> a faithful man, and feared God above many. <hi type="super">3</hi> And I said unto them, Let not the gates of Jerusalem be opened until the sun be hot; and while they stand by, let them shut the doors, and bar <hi type="italic">them:</hi> and appoint watches of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, every one in his watch, and every one <hi type="italic">to be</hi> over against his house. <hi type="super">4</hi> Now the city <hi type="italic">was</hi> large and great: but the people <hi type="italic">were</hi> few therein, and the houses <hi type="italic">were</hi> not builded. <div eID="gen8843" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8844" type="x-p"/> God saith concerning his church (<reference osisRef="Isa.62.6">Isa. lxii. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">I have set watchmen upon thy walls, O Jerusalem!</hi> This is Nehemiah's care here; for dead walls, without living watchmen, are but a poor defence to a city. <div eID="gen8844" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8845" type="x-p"/> I. He appointed <hi type="italic">the porters, singers, and Levites,</hi> in their places to their work. This is meant of their work in general, which was to attend the temple service; it had been neglected in some degree, but now was revived. God's worship is the defence of a place, and his ministers, when they mind their duty, are watchmen on the walls. Or, in particular, he ordered them to be ready against the wall was to be dedicated, that they might perform that service in an orderly and solemn manner; and the dedication of it was its strength. That is likely to be beneficial to us which is devoted to God. <div eID="gen8845" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8846" type="x-p"/> II. He appointed two governors or consuls, to whom he committed the care of the city, and gave them in charge to provide for the public peace and safety. Hanani, his brother, who came to him with the tidings of the desolations of Jerusalem, was one, a man of approved integrity and affection to his country; the other was Hananiah, who had been ruler of the palace: for he that has approved himself faithful in less shall be entrusted with more. Of this Hananiah it is said that he was a <hi type="italic">faithful man and one that feared God above many,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.7.2">v. 2</reference>. Note, 1. Among those who fear God truly there are some who fear him greatly, and excel others in the expressions and instances of that fear; and they are worthy a double portion of that honour which is due to those that <hi type="italic">fear the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.15.4">Ps. xv. 4</reference>. There were many in Jerusalem that feared God, but this good man was more eminent for religion and serious godliness than any. 2. Those that fear God must evidence it by their being faithful to all men and universally conscientious. 3. God's Jerusalem is then likely to flourish when those rule in it, and have charge of it, who excel in virtue, and are eminent both for godliness and honesty. It is supposed, by some, that Nehemiah was now about to return to the Persian court to have his commission renewed, and that he left these two worthy men in charge with the affairs of the city in his absence. Good governors, when and where they cannot act themselves, must be very careful whom they depute. <div eID="gen8846" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8847" type="x-p"/> III. He gave orders about the shutting of the gates and the guarding of the walls, <reference osisRef="Neh.7.3-Neh.7.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. See here, 1. What the present state of Jerusalem was. The city, in compass, was large and great. The walls enclosed the same ground as formerly; but much of it lay waste, for the houses were not built, few at least in comparison with what had been; so that Nehemiah walled the city in faith, and with an eye to that promise of the replenishing of it which God had lately made by the prophet, <reference osisRef="Zech.8.3-Zech.8.8">Zech. viii. 3</reference>, &c. Though the people were now few, he believed they would be multiplied, and therefore built the walls so as to make room for them; had he not depended upon this he might have thought walls without a city as great a reproach as a city without walls. 2. What was the care of Nehemiah for it. He ordered the rulers of the city themselves, (1.) To stand by, and see the city-gates shut up and barred every night; for in vain had they a wall if they were careless of their gates. (2.) To take care that they should not be opened in the morning till they could see that all was clear and quiet. (3.) To set sentinels upon the walls, or elsewhere, at convenient distances, who should, in case of the approach of the enemy, give timely notice to the city of the danger; and, as it came to their turn to watch, they must post themselves <hi type="italic">over against their own houses,</hi> because of them, it might be presumed, they would be in a particular manner careful. The public safety depends upon every one's particular care to guard himself and his own family against sin, that common enemy. It is every one's interest to watch, but many understand not their own interest; it is therefore incumbent upon magistrates to appoint watches. And as this people had lately found God with them in their building (else they would have built in vain), so now that the wall was built, no doubt, they were made sensible that <hi type="italic">except the Lord kept the city the watchman waked but in vain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.127.1">Ps. cxxvii. 1</reference>.

The Tirshatha gave to the treasure a thousand drams of gold, fifty basons, five hundred and thirty priests' garments. <hi type="super">71</hi> And <hi type="italic">some</hi> of the chief of the fathers gave to the treasure of the work twenty thousand drams of gold, and two thousand and two hundred pound of silver. <hi type="super">72</hi> And <hi type="italic">that</hi> which the rest of the people gave <hi type="italic">was</hi> twenty thousand drams of gold, and two thousand pound of silver, and threescore and seven priests' garments. <hi type="super">73</hi> So the priests, and the Levites, and the porters, and the singers, and <hi type="italic">some</hi> of the people, and the Nethinims, and all Israel, dwelt in their cities; and when the seventh month came, the children of Israel <hi type="italic">were</hi> in their cities. <div eID="gen8848" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8849" type="x-p"/> We have here another good project of Nehemiah's; for wise and zealous men will be always contriving something or other for the glory of God and the edification of his church. He knew very well that the safety of a city, under God, depends more upon the number and valour of the inhabitants than upon the height or strength of its walls; and therefore, observing that the people were few that dwelt in it, he thought fit to take an account of the people, that he might find what families had formerly had their settlement in Jerusalem, but were now removed into the country, that he might bring them back, and what families could in any other way be influenced by their religion, or by their business, to come and rebuild the houses in Jerusalem and dwell in them. So little reason have we to wish that we may be placed alone in the earth, or in Jerusalem itself, that much of our safety and comfort depends upon our neighbours and friends; the more the stronger, the more the merrier. It is the wisdom of the governors of a nation to keep the balance even between the city and country, that the metropolis be not so extravagantly large as to drain and impoverish the country, nor yet so weak as not to be able to protect it. Now observe, <div eID="gen8849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8850" type="x-p"/> I. Whence this good design of Nehemiah's came. He owns, <hi type="italic">My God put it into my heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Neh.7.5">v. 5</reference>. Note, Whatever good motion is in our minds, either prudent or pious, we must acknowledge it to come from God. It was he that <hi type="italic">put it into our hearts;</hi> for every good gift and every good work are from above. He gives knowledge; he gives grace; all is of him, and therefore all must be to him. What is done by human prudence must be ascribed to the direction of divine Providence; he that teaches the husbandman his discretion (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.26">Isa. xxviii. 26</reference>) teaches the statesman his. <div eID="gen8850" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8851" type="x-p"/> II. What method he took in prosecution of it. <div eID="gen8851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8852" type="x-p"/> 1. He called the rulers together, and the people, that he might have an account of the present state of their families—their number and strength, and where they were settled. It is probable that when he summoned them to come together he ordered them to bring such an account along with them out of their several districts. And I doubt they were not so many but that it might be soon done. <div eID="gen8852" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8853" type="x-p"/> 2. He reviewed the old <hi type="italic">register of the genealogy of those who came up at the first,</hi> and compared the present accounts with that; and here we have the repetition of that out of <reference osisRef="Ezra.2">Ezra 2</reference>. The title is the same here (<reference osisRef="Neh.7.6-Neh.7.7">v. 6, 7</reference>) as there (<reference osisRef="Neh.7.1-Neh.7.2">v. 1, 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">These are the children of the province,</hi> &c. Two things are here repeated and recorded a second time from thence—the names and numbers of their several families, and their oblations to the service of the temple. The repetition of these accounts may intimate to us the delight which the great God is pleased to take in the persons, families, and services of his spiritual Israel, and the particular notice he takes of them. He knows those that are his, knows them all, knows them by name, has his eye on the register of those children of the captivity, and does all according to the ancient counsel of his will concerning them. <div eID="gen8853" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8854" type="x-p"/> (1.) Here is an account of the heads of the several families that first came up, <reference osisRef="Neh.7.6-Neh.7.69">v. 6-69</reference>. As to this, [1.] Though it seem of little use to us now, yet then it was of great use, to compare what they had been with what they now were. We may suppose they were much increased by this time; but it would do well for them to remember their small beginnings, that they might acknowledge God in multiplying their families and building them up. By this means likewise their genealogies would be preserved, and the distinction of their families kept up, till the Messiah should come, and then an end be put to all their genealogies, which were preserved for his sake, but afterwards were endless. But, [2.] There are many differences in the numbers between this catalogue and that in Ezra. Most of them indeed are exactly the same, and some others within a very few under or over (one or two perhaps); and therefore I cannot think, as some do, that that was the number of these families at their first coming and this as they were now, which was at least forty years after (some make it much more); for we cannot suppose so many families to be not at all, or but little, altered in their numbers in all that time; therefore what differences there are we may suppose to arise either from the mistakes of transcribers, which easily happen in numbers, or from the diversity of the copies from which they were taken. Or perhaps one was the account of them when they set out from Babylon with Zerubbabel, the other when they came to Jerusalem. The sum totals are all just the same there and here, except of the singing-men and singing-women, which there are 200, here 245. These were not of such importance as that they should keep any strict account of them. <div eID="gen8854" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8855" type="x-p"/> (2.) Here is an account of the offerings which were given towards the work of God, <reference osisRef="Neh.7.70-Neh.7.72">v. 70</reference>, &c. This differs much from that in <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.68-Ezra.2.69">Ezra ii. 68, 69</reference>, and it may be questioned whether it refers to the same contribution; here the tirshatha, or chief governor, who there was not mentioned, begins the offering; and the single sum mentioned there exceeds all those here put together; yet it is probable that it was the same, but that followed one copy of the lists, this another; for the <reference osisRef="Neh.7.73 Ezra.2.70 Ezra.3.1">last verse</reference> is the same here that it was <reference osisRef="Neh.7.73 Ezra.2.70 Ezra.3.1">Ezra ii. 70, adding ch. iii. 1</reference>. Blessed be God that our faith and hope are not built upon the niceties of names and numbers, genealogy and chronology, but on the great things of the law and gospel. Whatever is given to the work of God, he is not unrighteous to forget it; nor shall even a cup of cold water, wherewith he is honoured, go without its reward.  <chapter eID="Neh.7"/> <div eID="gen8855" type="x-p"/>

entries.8c440aea8aa642d5fffeb30bb400ec1c7d4b54b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4333"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 7</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Neh.7.1-Neh.7.4">Ne 7:1-4</reference>. Nehemiah Commits the Charge of Jerusalem to Hanani and Hananiah.</title> <div sID="gen6279" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4333"/><hi type="bold">2. I gave my brother Hanani ... charge over Jerusalem--</hi>If, as is commonly supposed, Nehemiah was now contemplating a return to Shushan according to his promise, it was natural that he should wish to entrust the custody of Jerusalem and the management of its civic affairs to men on whose ability, experience, and fidelity, he could confide. Hanani, a near relative (<reference osisRef="Neh.1.2">Ne 1:2</reference>), was one, and with him was associated, as colleague, Hananiah, "the ruler of the palace"--that is, the marshal or chamberlain of the viceregal court, which Nehemiah had maintained in Jerusalem. The high religious principle, as well as the patriotic spirit of those two men, recommended them as pre-eminently qualified for being invested with an official trust of such peculiar importance.<div eID="gen6279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6280" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and feared God above many--</hi>The piety of Hananiah is especially mentioned as the ground of his eminent fidelity in the discharge of all his duties and, consequently, the reason of the confidence which Nehemiah reposed in him; for he was fully persuaded that Hananiah's fear of God would preserve him from those temptations to treachery and unfaithfulness which he was likely to encounter on the governor's departure from Jerusalem. <div eID="gen6280" type="x-p"/>
entries.aea366baa833203ec9054a5327f7591a0683a256: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4334"/><div sID="gen6281" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4334"/><hi type="bold">3. Let not the gates of Jerusalem be opened until the sun be hot, &c.--</hi>In the East it is customary to open the gates of a city at sunrise, and to bar them at sunset--a rule which is very rarely, and not except to persons of authority, infringed upon. Nehemiah recommended that the gates of Jerusalem should not be opened so early; a precaution necessary at a time when the enemy was practising all sorts of dangerous stratagems, to ensure that the inhabitants were all astir and enjoyed the benefit of clear broad daylight for observing the suspicious movements of any enemy. The propriety of regularly barring the gates at sunset was, in this instance, accompanied with the appointment of a number of the people to act as sentinels, each mounting guard in front of his own house. <div eID="gen6281" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f80fd1ccaa82fe5141890180e62c484e3c4f6bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4335"/><div sID="gen6282" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4335"/><hi type="bold">4. Now the city was large and great--</hi>The walls being evidently built on the old foundations, the city covered a large extent of surface, as all Oriental towns do, the houses standing apart with gardens and orchards intervening. This extent, in the then state of Jerusalem, was the more observable as the population was comparatively small, and the habitations of the most rude and simple construction--mere wooden sheds or coverings of loose, unmortared stones. <div eID="gen6282" type="x-p"/>
entries.c1cce391fa83c556a2a9eefed04e8166374b86e7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4336"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Neh.7.5-Neh.7.38">Ne 7:5-38</reference>. Genealogy of Those Who Came at the First Out of Babylon.</title> <div sID="gen6283" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4336"/><hi type="bold">5. my God put into mine heart to gather together the nobles, &c.--</hi>The arrangement about to be described, though dictated by mere common prudence, is, in accordance with the pious feelings of Nehemiah, ascribed not to his own prudence or reflection, but to the grace of God prompting and directing him. He resolved to prepare a register of the returned exiles, containing an exact record of the family and ancestral abode of every individual. While thus directing his attention, he discovered a register of the first detachment who had come under the care of Zerubbabel. It is transcribed in the following verses, and differs in some few particulars from that given in <reference osisRef="Ezra.2.1-Ezra.2.61">Ezr 2:1-61</reference>. But the discrepancy is sufficiently accounted for from the different circumstances in which the two registers were taken; that of Ezra having been made up at Babylon, while that of Nehemiah was drawn out in Judea, after the walls of Jerusalem had been rebuilt. The lapse of so many years might well be expected to make a difference appear in the catalogue, through death or other causes; in particular, one person being, according to Jewish custom, called by different names. Thus Hariph (<reference osisRef="Neh.7.24">Ne 7:24</reference>) is the same as Jorah (<reference osisRef="Ezra.2.18">Ezr 2:18</reference>), Sia (<reference osisRef="Neh.7.47">Ne 7:47</reference>) the same as Siaha (<reference osisRef="Ezra.2.44">Ezr 2:44</reference>), &c. Besides other purposes to which this genealogy of the nobles, rulers, and people was subservient, one leading object contemplated by it was to ascertain with accuracy the parties to whom the duty legally belonged of ministering at the altar and conducting the various services of the temple. For guiding to exact information in this important point of enquiry, the possession of the old register of Zerubbabel was invaluable. <div eID="gen6283" type="x-p"/>
entries.615dccecedfca5856bafd27cba0bdae3ebe1f846: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4337"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Neh.7.39-Neh.7.73">Ne 7:39-73</reference>. Of the Priests.</title> <div sID="gen6284" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4337"/><hi type="bold">39. The priests--</hi>It appears that only four of the courses of the priests returned from the captivity; and that the course of Abia (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.5">Lu 1:5</reference>) is not in the list. But it must be noticed that these four courses were afterwards divided into twenty-four, which retained the names of the original courses which David appointed. <div eID="gen6284" type="x-p"/>
entries.50f9db592a77d920a2dd1bfe72fbee19267074b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4338"/><div sID="gen6285" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4338"/><hi type="bold">70. And some of the chief of the fathers, &c.--</hi>With <reference osisRef="Neh.7.69">Ne 7:69</reference> the register ends, and the thread of Nehemiah's history is resumed. He was the tirshatha, or governor, and the liberality displayed by him and some of the leading men for the suitable equipment of the ministers of religion, forms the subject of the remaining portion of the chapter. Their donations consisted principally in garments. This would appear a singular description of gifts to be made by any one among us; but, in the East, a present of garments, or of any article of use, is conformable to the prevailing sentiments and customs of society.<div eID="gen6285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6286" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drams of gold--</hi>that is, darics. A daric was a gold coin of ancient Persia, worth £1 5s. <div eID="gen6286" type="x-p"/>
entries.158286b71c79df68e409497f090c2ea2510eaa9b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4339"/><div sID="gen6287" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4339"/><hi type="bold">71. pound of silver--</hi>that is, mina (sixty shekels, or £9). <div eID="gen6287" type="x-p"/>
entries.954c2da4bfb08a0d74bbd710f5a50af1dbc22e91: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4340"/><div sID="gen6288" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4340"/><hi type="bold">73. So ... all Israel, dwelt in their cities--</hi>The utility of these genealogical registers was thus found in guiding to a knowledge of the cities and localities in each tribe to which every family anciently belonged. <chapter eID="Neh.7"/>

entries.92ce84c1996c3b152e067e8bfd2b80f08fbe4977: <div eID="gen15111" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen15112" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15113" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15113" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15112" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15114" type="x-p"/> Nehemiah makes use of proper precautions in guarding the city gates, <reference osisRef="Neh.7.1-Neh.7.4">Neh 7:1-4</reference>. He proposes to reckon the people according to their genealogies; and finds a register of those who came out of Babylon, with Zerubbabel, <reference osisRef="Neh.7.5-Neh.7.7">Neh 7:5-7</reference>. A transcript of the register, vv. 8-60. Account of those who came from other provinces; and of priests who, because they could not show their register, were put away from the priesthood as polluted, <reference osisRef="Neh.7.61-Neh.7.65">Neh 7:61-65</reference>. The sum total of the congregation: of their men-servants and maid-servants; singing men and women; horses, mules, camels, and asses, <reference osisRef="Neh.7.66-Neh.7.69">Neh 7:66-69</reference>. The sums given by different persons for the work, <reference osisRef="Neh.7.70-Neh.7.72">Neh 7:70-72</reference>. All betake themselves to their several cities, <reference osisRef="Neh.7.73">Neh 7:73</reference>.
entries.361dea86cef6da1a39536ffac5f9be369ce61d2b: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen15114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15115" type="x-p"/> My brother Hanani - This was the person who gave Nehemiah the account of the desolate state of the Jews, <reference osisRef="Neh.1.2">Neh 1:2</reference>. He is now made ruler of Jerusalem, probably because Nehemiah was about to return to the Persian court. And he found this man to be one in whom he could trust: <div eID="gen15115" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15116" type="x-p"/> 1. Because he was a faithful man - one who had a proper belief in God, his government, and his protection; and being devoted to the interests of his people, would be faithful in the discharge of his office. <div eID="gen15116" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15117" type="x-p"/> 2. Because he feared God above many - was the most religious person in the congregation; would govern according to the laws; would take care of the interests of pure religion; would not oppress, take bribes, nor abuse his authority; but act in all things as one who had the fear of God continually before his eyes. These are the proper qualifications of a governor.
entries.67cddd820eff26bebcd4eede87257b81097d35e8: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen15117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15118" type="x-p"/> Until the sun be hot - The meaning of this is, the gates were not to be opened before sunrise, and always shut at sunset. This is the custom to the present day in many of the cities of the East if a traveler arrives after sunset, he finds the gates shut; and on no consideration will they open them till the next morning, so that those who come late are obliged to lodge in the plain, or under the walls. <div eID="gen15118" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15119" type="x-p"/> Every one - over against his house - Each was obliged to guard that part of the wall that was opposite to his own dwelling.
entries.81fc6d8587fc14a11df83f23c0f2ae7298eee603: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen15119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15120" type="x-p"/> The houses were not builded - The city was not yet rebuilt, only a row of houses in the inside of the wall all round.
entries.7142506598bfc82ee5dafa62ba8ecae434e07b68: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen15120" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15121" type="x-p"/> God put into mine heart - With this good man every good thing was of God. If he purposed any good, it was because God put it into his heart; if he did any good, it was because the good hand of his God was upon him; if he expected any good, it was because he earnestly prayed God to remember him for good. Thus, in all his ways he acknowledged God, and God directed all his steps.
entries.0fe415692f9a6ec66cc51f7fc0ca6f5467b3f0c2: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen15121" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15122" type="x-p"/> Who came with Zerubbabel - The register which he found was that of the persons only who came long before Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Joshua the son of Josedek, which register could not answer in every respect to the state of the people then. Several persons and families were no doubt dead, and others had arrived since. Nehemiah probably altered it only in such parts, leaving the body of it as it was before; and this will account for the difference between it and the register that is found in Ezra, chap. 2.
entries.f94df8ce9c2d50a299bc54bd015fb7e6526dbadb: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen15122" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15123" type="x-p"/> The children of Parosh - As this chapter is almost entirely the same with the second chapter of the book of Ezra, it is not necessary to add any thing to what is said there; and to that chapter, and the accompanying notes, the reader is requested to refer.
entries.725925d4619f89ddc0dcc4d6fef954e98c3942b3: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen15123" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15124" type="x-p"/> The children of Bigval, two thousand threescore and seven - Some MSS. read two thousand and sixty-six, as in <reference osisRef="Ezr.2.14">Ezr 2:14</reference>.
entries.8bb661c879faf118d95aca5090fc6452298fe86d: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen15124" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15125" type="x-p"/> The men of the other Nebo - The word other is not in the parallel place, <reference osisRef="Ezr.2.29">Ezr 2:29</reference>, and is wanting in many of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. This Nebo is supposed to be the same as Nob or Nobah, in the tribe of Benjamin.
entries.61c580d636d07c387bbe8398377ecfafd1a6c35e: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen15125" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15126" type="x-p"/> The other Elam - To distinguish him from the Elam mentioned <reference osisRef="Neh.7.12">Neh 7:12</reference>.
entries.db01064730617f30f6caa970eaf0ca1e1310e8d3: <hi type="bold">Verse 54</hi> <div eID="gen15126" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15127" type="x-p"/> The children of Mehida - Many of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS., have Mehira.
entries.7b1cd31755728d079929941c0471d47cc8517feb: <hi type="bold">Verse 68</hi> <div eID="gen15127" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15128" type="x-p"/> Their horses, etc. - The whole of this verse is wanting in fifty of Kennicott's MSS., and in twenty-nine of those of De Rossi, in the edition of Rab. Chayim, 1525, in the Roman Edit. of the Septuagint; also in the Syriac and in the Arabic. It should however be observed, that the Arabic omits the whole list, having nothing of the chapter but the first five verses. The whole is found in the parallel place, <reference osisRef="Ezr.2.66">Ezr 2:66</reference>. Calmet's note on this passage is incorrect.
entries.37de06d62261910aa7c3aed92bdb1b883b03b5d8: <hi type="bold">Verse 69</hi> <div eID="gen15128" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15129" type="x-p"/> Their camels, four hundred thirty and five - After this verse St. <div eID="gen15129" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15130" type="x-p"/> Jerome has inserted the following words in the Vulgate: - <div eID="gen15130" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15131" type="x-p"/> Hucusque refertur quid in commentario scriptum fuerit; exin Nehemiae historia texitur. "Thus far do the words extend which were written in the register; what follows belongs to the history of Nehemiah." <div eID="gen15131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15132" type="x-p"/> But this addition is not found either in the Hebrew or any of the ancient versions. It is wanting also in the Complutum and Paris Polyglots, but is in the Editio Prima of the Vulgate.
entries.80fb677266bcf33fb04e7629308a114f00b22b6a: <hi type="bold">Verse 70</hi> <div eID="gen15132" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15133" type="x-p"/> The Tirshatha gave - The Septuagint, particularly the copy in the Codex Alexandrinus, intimates that this sum was given to the Tirshatha, or Nehemiah: Και τῳ Αθερσαθᾳ εδωκαν εις θησαυρον, And to the Athersatha they gave for the treasure, etc. <div eID="gen15133" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15134" type="x-p"/> For the meaning of the word Tirshatha, see on <reference osisRef="Ezr.2.63">Ezr 2:63</reference> (note).
entries.7d276a3a1c711051261b6dbefbf42aec93fdbca9: <hi type="bold">Verse 71</hi> <div eID="gen15134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15135" type="x-p"/> Two thousand and two hundred pounds - The Septuagint has two thousand Three hundred minae of silver.
entries.168a0749f27e9e316e3596bedd2089e55552333d: <hi type="bold">Verse 73</hi> <div eID="gen15135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15136" type="x-p"/> All Israel, dwelt in their cities - It was in reference to this particularly that the public registers were examined; for by them they found the different families, and consequently the cities, villages, etc., which belonged to them, according to the ancient division of the lands. It seems that the examination of the registers occupied about a month; for as soon as the walls were finished, which was in the sixth month, (Elul), <reference osisRef="Neh.6.15">Neh 6:15</reference>, Nehemiah instituted the examination mentioned in this chapter, <reference osisRef="Neh.7.5">Neh 7:5</reference>; and by the concluding verse we find that the different families had got into their paternal cities in the seventh month, Tisri, answering to a part of our September and October. Thus the register determined every thing: there was no room for complaint, and none to accuse the governor of partiality.  <chapter eID="Neh.7"/> <div eID="gen15136" type="x-p"/>

entries.12c2135fe9d44fb07aa6fcf1cc4ba901ba3af19c: <div eID="gen6579" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">II. Nehemiah’s Further Exertions in Behalf of the Community - <reference osisRef="Neh.7.1">Neh 7:1</reference></title> <div sID="gen6580" type="x-p"/> The building of the wall being now concluded, Nehemiah first made arrangements for securing the city against hostile attacks (<reference osisRef="Neh.7.1-Neh.7.3">Neh 7:1-3</reference>); then took measures to increase the inhabitants of Jerusalem (7:4-73 and <reference osisRef="Neh.11.1">Neh 11:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="Neh.11.2">Neh 11:2</reference>); and finally endeavoured to fashion domestic and civil life according to the precepts of the law (<reference osisRef="Neh.8.10">Neh 8-10</reference>), and, on the occasion of the solemn dedication of the wall, to set in order the services of the Levites (Neh 12).<hi type="italic">The watching of the city provided for</hi>. - <div eID="gen6580" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6581" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Neh.7.1">Neh 7:1</reference> <div eID="gen6581" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6582" type="x-p"/> When the wall was built, Nehemiah set up the doors in the gates, to complete the fortification of Jerusalem (comp. <reference osisRef="Neh.6.1">Neh 6:1</reference>). Then were the gatekeepers, the singers, and the Levites entrusted with the care (הפּקד, <hi type="italic">praefici</hi>; comp. <reference osisRef="Neh.12.14">Neh 12:14</reference>). The care of watching the walls and gates is meant in this connection. According to ancient appointment, it was the duty of the doorkeepers to keep watch over the house of God, and to open and close the gates of the temple courts; comp. <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.17-1Chr.9.19">1Ch 9:17-19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.12">1Ch 26:12</reference>-19. The singers and the Levites appointed to assist the priests, on the contrary, had, in ordinary times, nothing to do with the service of watching. Under the present extraordinary circumstances, however, Nehemiah committed also to these two organized corporations the task of keeping watch over the walls and gates of the city, and placed them under the command of his brother Hanani, and of Hananiah the ruler of the citadel. This is expressed by the words, <reference osisRef="Neh.7.2">Neh 7:2</reference> : I gave Hanani ... and Hananiah ... charge over Jerusalem. הבּירה is the fortress or citadel of the city lying to the north of the temple (see rem. on <reference osisRef="Neh.2.8">Neh 2:8</reference>), in which was probably located the royal garrison, the commander of which was in the service of the Persian king. The choice of this man for so important a charge is explained by the additional clause: “for he was a faithful man, and feared God above many.” The כּ before אישׁ is the so-called Caph <hi type="italic">veritatis</hi>, which expresses a comparison with the idea of the matter: like a man whom one may truly call faithful. מרבּים is comparative: more God-fearing than many.
entries.9ab0b2126917d4f10ed8fb7dfc0a95e438dcb538: <reference osisRef="Neh.7.3">Neh 7:3</reference> <div eID="gen6582" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6583" type="x-p"/> The Chethiv ויאמר is both here and <reference osisRef="Neh.5.9">Neh 5:9</reference> certainly a clerical error for the Keri ואמר, though in this place, at all events, we might read ויּאמר, it was said to them. “The gates of Jerusalem are not to be opened till the sun be hot; and while they (the watch) are yet at their posts, they are to shut the doors and lock them; and ye shall appoint watches of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, some to be at their watch-posts, others before their house.” יגיפוּ in Hebrew is used only here, though more frequently in the Talmud, of closing the doors. אחז, to make fast, i.e., to lock, as more frequently in Syriac. The <hi type="italic">infin. absol</hi>. העמיד instead of the <hi type="italic">temp. fin</hi>. is emphatic: and you are to appoint. The sense is: the gates are to be occupied before daybreak by the Levites (singers and other Levites) appointed to guard them, and not opened till the sun is hot and the watch already at their posts, and to be closed in the evening before the departure of the watch. After the closing of the gates, i.e., during the night, the inhabitants of Jerusalem are to keep watch for the purpose of defending the city from any kind of attack, a part occupying the posts, and the other part watching before their (each before his own) house, so as to be at hand to defend the city.
entries.60dc4f7af9013228f6a57f13dfe6ea11ad8411f4: <reference osisRef="Neh.7.4">Neh 7:4</reference> <div eID="gen6583" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6584" type="x-p"/> The measures taken by Nehemiah for increasing the number of the inhabitants of Jerusalem. - <reference osisRef="Neh.7.4">Neh 7:4</reference> The city was spacious and great, and the people few therein, and houses were not built. ידים רחבת, broads on both sides, that is, regarded from the centre towards either the right or left hand. The last clause does not say that there were no houses at all, for the city had been re-inhabited for ninety years; but only that houses had not been built in proportion to the size of the city, that there was still much unoccupied space on which houses might be built.
entries.036967684ce342c2289971a669131fcb4a8e7f76: <reference osisRef="Neh.7.5-Neh.7.73">Neh 7:5-73</reference> <div eID="gen6584" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6585" type="x-p"/> And God put into my heart, i.e., God inspired me with the resolution; comp. Neh 2:12. What resolution, is declared by the sentences following, which detail its execution. The resolution to gather together the nobles and rulers of the people for the purpose of making a list of their kinsmen, and thus to obtain a basis for the operations contemplated for increasing the inhabitants of Jerusalem. והסּגנים החרים are combined, as in Neh 2:16. On התיחשׂ, comp. 1Ch 5:17. <div eID="gen6585" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6586" type="x-p"/> While this resolve was under consideration, Nehemiah found the register, i.e., the genealogical registry, of those who came up at first (from Babylon). בּראשׁונה, at the beginning, i.e., with Zerubbabel and Joshua under Cyrus (Ezra 2), and not subsequently with Ezra (Ezra 7). “And I found written therein.” These words introduce the list now given. This list, vv. 6-73 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, is identical with that in Ezra 2, and has been already discussed in our remarks on that chapter.  <chapter eID="Neh.7"/> <div eID="gen6586" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. VII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 NOw it came to pass when the wall was built, and I had set up the doors, and the porters, and the singers, and the Levites were appointed <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> When I had taken order that the Levites should be sum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />moned from all places to celebrate the dedication of the Wall, as it was done, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 12. 27.</ns0:note>;</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 That I gave my brother Hanani <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Of whom see <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1. 1, 2.</ns0:note>, and Hanani<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ah the ruler of the palace <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Of <ns0:hi>Nehemiah</ns0:hi>'s Court, justly so called, because he lived in great splendor, and like a Vice-Roy, though it was wholly at his own charge.</ns0:note>, charge over Jerusalem <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">To preserve its peace and safety, and to take particular care of the shutting the Gates of the City.</ns0:note>: (for he <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">To wit, <ns0:hi>Hananiah</ns0:hi> last mentioned: for it was needless to say any thing in commendation of <ns0:hi>Hanani,</ns0:hi> who had shewn his Piety and Zeal for God and his Country, in taking a tedious jour<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ney from <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> to <ns0:hi>Shushan,</ns0:hi> to inform <ns0:hi>Nehemiah</ns0:hi> of the sad Estate of <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> and to implore his helping hand to relieve it, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 1.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> a faithful man <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">He chose not Magistrates and Officers out of any partial or carnal respects to his own Kindred, or Acquaintance, or Favourites, but from true Piety and Prudence, such as were fittest for, and would be most faithful in their Employments.</ns0:note>, and feared God <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">This is added as the ground and reason, both why he was faithful, and why <ns0:hi>Nehemiah</ns0:hi> put such Trust and Confidence in him, because he knew that the fear of God would keep him from yielding to those temptations to perfidiousness which he was likely to meet with when <ns0:hi>Nehemiah</ns0:hi> was gone, and against which a man destitute of Gods fear hath no suf<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ficient sence.</ns0:note> above many <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">More than most men did, or, above the com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mon pitch of piety.</ns0:note>.)</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 And I said unto them, Let not the gates of Jeru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />salem be opened, until the son be hot <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Till it be clear and broad day; when Enemies approach<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing may be discovered, and the people of the City will be ready for the defence in case of an assault.</ns0:note>; and while they <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> The watches appoint<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed to that end, as is manifest from the following words</ns0:note> stand by, let them shut the doors, and bar <ns0:hi>them,</ns0:hi> and appoint watches of the Inhabitants of Jerusalem, every one in his watch, and every one to be over against his house <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Eve<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry one in his turn, keeping watch with others in that watching<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />place which is next to his house.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 Now the city was <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>broad of hands,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>spaces.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> large and great: but the peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> few therein, and the houses <ns0:hi>were</ns0:hi> not built <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Not all, nor compleatly built; but only some sleight Buildings of Boards or Stones were made for the present use of the generality of the People.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 And my God put into mine heart <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">This Action, though meerly prudential, he doth not ascribe to himself, or his own wit, but to the Gift, and Grace of God di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />recting and inclining him to it.</ns0:note>, to gather together the nobles and the rulers, and the people <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Not only for the particular end here mentioned, but for divers other weighty purposes and mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ters, of which the following Chapters treat.</ns0:note>, that they might be reckoned by genealogy <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">That so it might appear to what Families each person belonged, and where their ancient Habitations lay, which for a great number of them were in the City, the replenishing of which was now his design.</ns0:note>, and I found a register of the genealogy of them which came up at the first <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">To wit, with Zerubbabel, as it follows, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 7. But this following Cata<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />logue differs in some particulars from that <ns0:hi>Ezra</ns0:hi> 2. of which see the notes there.</ns0:note>, and found written therein;</ns0:p>
